findings.evidence: Page 42: "A token’s K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled." Page 43 Fig 2.1 caption: "each step reads the cached K/V, appends the new K/V, and samples the next token."
findings.issue: The prose and figure caption describe two different append timings. The prose says a token’s K/V is appended when that token is the input (one step after it was sampled). The Fig 2.1 caption says each decode step "reads the cached K/V, appends the new K/V, and samples the next token" without clarifying that the "new K/V" appended is the current input token’s, not the just-sampled next token’s. Because the figure is the book’s canonical end-to-end pipeline and is reused conceptually in later chapters, this ambiguity can mislead readers about KV-cache growth ordering.
findings.fix_instruction: Revise the Fig 2.1 caption to match the prose: state explicitly that each decode step takes the previously sampled token as input, computes and appends that input token’s K/V, attends over the cache, and then samples the next token; the just-sampled token’s K/V is appended on the following step. Ensure the figure labels distinguish "input token" from "sampled token".

findings.evidence: Page 56 §2.3 arithmetic details: "With a TPOT budget of ~25 ms per token, the aggregate required bandwidth is Breq = Mweights / τ = 140 GB / 0.025 s = 5,600 GB/s = 5.6 TB/s [canonical scenario][DERIVED]. A single NVIDIA H100 HBM3 delivers ~3.35 TB/s peak bandwidth [1P][FACT]. Since 5.6 > 3.35, under this batch-1-equivalent weight-streaming model one H100 cannot supply the required aggregate weight-read rate — the decode phase is HBM-bandwidth-bound [canonical scenario][DERIVED]."
findings.issue: The sentence "the decode phase is HBM-bandwidth-bound" is stated immediately after a hypothetical single-device comparison, but the chapter itself (and Table 2-2) later insists that this is an illustrative single-device roofline point, not the canonical host verdict. The local wording overgeneralizes the conclusion before the caveat is supplied in the next sentence. This is a prose-clarity and scope issue: a reader skimming the worked example can take away a false host-level conclusion.
findings.fix_instruction: Reword to: "under this batch-1-equivalent single-device weight-streaming model, one H100 cannot supply the required aggregate weight-read rate; this is an illustrative single-device roofline point, not the canonical 8×H100 host’s bandwidth verdict (see Table 2-2 and §2.5)." Keep the host-level verdict separate from the hypothetical single-device comparison.

findings.evidence: Printed p. 56, Table 2-2 scope note: "Basis of these intensity figures, so the chapters reconcile:* every value here divides the linear-term prefill FLOPs, 2NL, by weight bytes. Adding the attention FLOPs to the numerator instead raises the weight-only value to ~10.8K FLOP/byte (the figure Ch 6, Table 6-1 quotes), while adding the ~24 GB KV write to the denominator is the correction that gives ~7,850."
findings.issue: Internal contradiction: the sentence claims 'every value here divides the linear-term prefill FLOPs, 2NL, by weight bytes' and then attributes ~7,850 FOP/byte to 'adding the ~24 GB KV write to the denominator.' But 1.29 PFLOP ÷ (140 GB + 24.1 GB) = 1.29e15 ÷ 1.641e11 ≈ 7,860 FLOP/byte — this divides by (weight + KV) bytes, NOT by weight bytes alone. The very next sentence says 'The two corrections act on different terms, so they are not competing estimates; all three bases sit far to the right of the ~295 ridge,' which acknowledges the three values use different bases — directly contradicting the earlier claim that 'every value here' shares one basis. A reader following the stated methodology (linear FLOPs ÷ weight bytes = 9,200) cannot reproduce 7,850.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite the basis note to state explicitly which numerator and which denominator produce each of the three values: (i) 9,200 = linear FLOPs ÷ weight bytes; (ii) 10,800 = (linear + attention) FLOPs ÷ weight bytes; (iii) 7,850 = linear FLOPs ÷ (weight + KV) bytes. Remove the claim that 'every value here' divides by weight bytes alone.
